#10429. What AI Gets Wrong About the Front End, and Why You Still Need to Know

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

Then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

That’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:

Build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:

With some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot shows the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

The real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

Here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

The buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the new product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

Those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern

I’d revise the original prompt like this:

Build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the new product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

The extra detail also gives you a review plan. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:

AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

Each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

The next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

#10424. Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Beyond food storage, the same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk.

A second wave of attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe this week has heightened concerns about the broader "cold chain's" vulnerability to similar attacks, given that supermarkets aren't the only businesses that rely on cold storage.

As in mid-October, an unknown threat actor appears to have gained access to refrigeration controllers at multiple European supermarkets and switched the systems to defrost mode, raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing food spoilage.

Reporting by the BBC, Reuters, CNBC, and other outlets suggests the latest attacks were smaller in scope compared with the first wave in October that affected more than 700 retail and grocery stores, primarily in France. A smaller number of stores in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Poland and Spain were also caught up in the October attacks.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

BBC reported the new attacks as impacting "dozens of supermarkets" in seven European countries including Belgium, Luxembourg, Estonia, Ireland, Sweden and Finland. Spokespersons from several supermarket chains that include France's Carrefour, Belgium's Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt Group, and Sweden's Coop chains confirmed varying but relatively limited impacts from the new attacks.

In a Nov. 2 statement, Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting its refrigeration systems had impacted 15 out of 700 stores in Belgium. In an undated statement, US-based Copeland, which manufactures technologies for regulating commercial refrigeration systems, alluded to a cybersecurity incident affecting refrigeration systems in France, which it said related to a discontinued generation of supervisory controllers.

No individual or group has claimed responsibility for either the first or the second wave of attacks, and the motivation behind it remains a mystery. European authorities are currently investigating the attacks.

Researchers, including those at France's CERT, have linked the hacks so far to Internet-connected refrigeration controllers made by Denmark-based Danfoss, Italy-based Dixell, and Copeland. Organizations using these controllers often connect them to the Internet to enable remote maintenance and support, but in doing so also potentially expose them to unauthorized access and remote attack by threat actors.

Risks include unpatched vulnerabilities in these technologies that attackers can exploit, like three in Danfoss' AK-SM 800A controllers that researchers at Claroty disclosed this August and another two they reported the same month in Copeland controllers. Weak configurations and poor security hygiene are other major problems.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

"Misconfigurations and systemic hygiene failures represent the vast majority of the threat surface," says John Gallagher, vice president at operational technology (OT) and Internet of Things (IoT) security vendor Viakoo. "While unpatched vulnerabilities exist in older firmware, they are rendered dangerous only because basic architectural hygiene was skipped, especially [when] making them Internet-facing."

Common mistakes that include widespread use of default passwords, vendor-shared service codes, or static credentials across hundreds of locations make brute-forcing trivial, Gallagher adds.

The weaknesses are not confined to supermarket refrigeration systems. The same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk, according to security experts.

Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer (CTO) at Claroty, points out that "pharmaceutical storage and distribution, food distribution centers, and industrial facilities all rely on connected operational technology to maintain precise environmental conditions."

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

The level of exposure will vary depending on how these systems are deployed, connected, and secured. But many organizations that rely on remotely accessible refrigeration or temperature-control equipment face similar challenges around asset visibility, third-party access, and securing legacy systems, Tufts says. "The same types of weaknesses can exist across different industries, even if the equipment and operational requirements differ."

The potential consequences of a compromise, Tufts says, can vary by sector.

"A disruption to pharmaceutical storage could compromise temperature-sensitive medicines, while an incident affecting food distribution could lead to spoilage and supply chain disruptions," he notes. "Industrial environments may face additional operational consequences depending on the materials and processes involved."

The supermarket attacks are a reminder that refrigeration and temperature-control systems are part of essential operations and not just back-of-house equipment, Tufts adds. Organizations should identify these assets and know how they connect to the Internet and third parties.

"Where remote access is necessary, use a VPN, strong authentication, or a centralized secure-access tool with session tracking." Changing default passwords, keeping firmware current, and segmenting are also recommended security practices, he says.

Gallagher says that while it's unclear how the attacks on the commercial refrigeration systems played out, the most straightforward theory is the threat actor likely compiled a target list by scanning the public Internet for specific controller fingerprints, such as those tied to Danfoss, Dixell, and Copeland. They then likely deployed an automated script across that target list to exploit known web vulnerabilities or push default credentials, triggering the defrost mode simultaneously.

Gallagher says the same attacks that worked on commercial refrigeration systems can potentially work across almost any form of OT and IoT systems. That's because these systems often are managed outside of IT, lack automated controls to keep firmware and passwords updated, and have porous network borders. "The growth over the last three years in operational ransomware and in cyberattacks causing physical damage shows that these attacks are on the rise and not specific to any one kind of system."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#10423. Kevin O’Leary tells Gen Z: ‘Every generation has had whiners like you’

Shark Tank investor and businessman Kevin O’Leary is at odds with Gen Z, who say building wealth and success is harder for their generation than it was for his.

In Jubilee Media’s latest Surrounded video—an online series where a single public figure faces 25 individuals with opposing viewpoints—O’Leary, known as “Mr. Wonderful,” takes on a slate of questions regarding success and wealth.

But it’s one particular conversation in the nearly two-hour-long video that has gained traction on social media.

When the discussion turned to O’Leary’s assertion that “if you want to be successful, work-life balance comes second,” one participant pushed back on how realistic that advice is today.

“We used to have work-life balance—we don’t have that anymore,” one of the participants told O’Leary. “My question to you is, how do you believe that our generation is supposed to be successful and have a work-life balance if we can’t even afford what success would look like, which is owning a home and not being straddled by student loans and medical debt.”

O’Leary quickly replied, “Every single generation has had whiners like you in it. Each generation is surprised to find out things change in the economy all the time.”

Twenty years ago, O’Leary continued, a liberal arts or humanities degree could be considered an “economic disaster,” whereas today, videographers and storytellers are “making anywhere from $200,000 to $400,000 working for corporations.”

‘The kids . . . have totally given up’

As the clip made the rounds on social media, some agreed with O’Leary’s stance on the matter, echoing the age-old claim that younger generations are less willing to work than their older counterparts.

“Not a huge Kevin O’Leary guy, but the kids he’s speaking with have totally given up. They need to keep pushing, they break through or change careers,” one user said on X.

But for most, Mr. Wonderful’s comments came across as disconnected from reality.

“With a straight face, Kevin said “photographers, videographers are making $200-$400k a year.” Out of touch doesn’t even begin to describe this guy’s ignorance,” one user replied on YouTube.

“Kevin O’Leary needs to go walk in the shoes of a middle-class American for a week. He has no idea what he’s talking about,” another added on X.

For others, the conversation further highlighted the tensions between generations.

A user on X added: “Kevin’s generation got theirs, bought houses cheap, got money to build businesses, got cheap college, then changed the rules to fuck every other generation after them.”

The video and the discourse surrounding it also pointed to a larger problem: Neither side can reach consensus.

A user added: “Problem is, the truth is somewhere in the middle of both tales being told, and nobody wants to acknowledge that their respective sides are both overstating the opposing ends of the equation.”

#10421. How to Reduce Hallucinations in LLMs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

Newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:

The traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:

Every version calls the model through one small helper:

We're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply said it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

The model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:

Delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data says nothing about price matching:

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:

Zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

If all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:

Every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:

If a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

This script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:

The check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:

No model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

It cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:

The model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

#10419. The FAA’s ground stop has a simple culprit. Its causes may not

On Friday afternoon, L3Harris Technologies was doing what it has done at Federal Aviation Administration facilities month after month: moving a communications line off decades-old copper and onto fiber, work that federal auditors count as part of a $12.5 billion overhaul of the country’s air traffic control system.

Shortly after a technician installed a new router at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device began pumping out data—so much that the flood disrupted communications at 17 of the 22 so-called en route centers that handle high-altitude traffic.

At 3:36 p.m. Eastern, with about 3,500 planes in the air, the FAA held all departures nationwide. The stop lasted more than four hours, until 8:15 p.m. Airlines canceled more than 5,000 flights by Saturday and about 1,500 more on Sunday as they repositioned crews and aircraft. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the system that sends safety notices to pilots failed.

“We haven’t determined what the fault was,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a Saturday news conference. Investigators are trying to establish whether L3Harris installed or configured the router incorrectly, or whether the equipment itself was at fault. Adam Bauer, a spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns router maker Juniper Networks, told Fast Company its devices appeared to have worked as intended. “Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured.”

But the failure exposed weaknesses the FAA has been warned about for years: a contractor that has run the FAA’s network since 2002 and has a record of outages, an integrator the agency’s own staff rated a financial risk, a technician workforce the FAA admits is understaffed, and a $12.5 billion overhaul that auditors say is racing ahead without a master schedule. There is no evidence yet that any of them caused Friday’s failure.

Still, some critics see Friday’s chaos as years of warnings come true. “The sad fact is this has happened before,” Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general, told NPR’s Weekend Edition.

The sprawling network of copper and fiber that carries the country’s air traffic communications across roughly 4,400 FAA sites still runs largely on technology that dates back decades. Some older equipment, including radar, requires replacement parts that can only be obtained through online auction websites or made with 3D printers. In 2023, an FAA-commissioned panel of outside experts warned that the condition of the agency’s facilities and equipment was “elevating system risk to unsustainable levels.” The agency under President Joe Biden had commissioned another group of aviation experts to examine air traffic control in October 2024, but weeks after Trump took office, the group learned it was being disbanded, The Washington Post reported. 

Last May, Duffy said the FAA was speeding up its overhaul of the system under a program called BNATCS, or the Brand New Air Traffic Control System. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort, which aims to modernize the telecom network by the end of 2028, before the end of Trump’s term, and 21 months ahead of an earlier September 2030 target.

In September, the Government Accountability Office released its latest report on the overhaul. The FAA was moving at an unprecedented speed, auditors said, but without a reliable lifecycle cost estimate or an integrated master schedule. Instead, auditors counted 11,389 separate project schedules that had not been coordinated, so different programs were booked to visit the same sites repeatedly or in ways that risk “excessive disruptions to air traffic control operations” and could jeopardize the FAA’s “aggressive deployment schedule.” Delays, in turn, could leave controllers reliant on outdated systems that are prone to failure, and “lead to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, and safety incidents.”

The GAO auditors also found the agency had exempted the effort from nearly all of its standard acquisition rules. Schedule pressure on federal programs can lead teams to skip or compress testing, they warned. “In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions,” the GAO wrote.

The incident has also drawn attention to Peraton, the Herndon, Va.-based defense contractor hired last December to manage the broader overhaul, under a contract with a $1.5 billion ceiling. Politico reported in June that one lobbyist—a former Duffy spokesperson who sits on the board of a nonprofit linked to the Transportation Secretary—lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. (The FAA has said that Duffy played no role in the company’s selection.)

By August, FAA officials were frustrated with Peraton’s performance, according to a September Politico report, citing people familiar with the matter who described slipping schedules and a contractor that was not managing the project. Peraton was “not sophisticated with how the FAA works” and was being asked to sprint from the start, one person told Politico. The same person said the FAA was partly to blame, accusing the agency of blocking Peraton’s efforts to work with its own staff.

As the FAA began its investigation into the cause of the router issues on Saturday, Schiavo told NPR that uncoordinated schedules and a rush to patch the system had made such a failure predictable. “What did the GAO conclude? That it will result in air traffic outages and disruptions. And there we are.”

The FAA and L3Harris take different approaches to scheduling 

The trouble first showed up as interruptions at the FAA’s Indianapolis center, as a surge of data flooded the network’s older routers. A flurry of erratic radar feeds and communication drop-offs with aircraft led officials to order a ground stop. Soon troubleshooters traced the issue to the El Dorado router and to a second one at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas; when both were cut off from the network, the problems stopped. Officials have zeroed in on a feature on the new Juniper routers that broadcast data more widely than necessary. The FAA has since switched the feature off on all of its Juniper routers. The two suspect routers are being tested in Florida with help from Juniper and Cisco engineers, L3Harris and the FBI. 

“Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration?” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford asked on Saturday, adding that the agency would have to rethink how it carries out upgrades.

Asked why the work was done on a busy Friday afternoon, Duffy cited the urgency of the upgrades and said the site was far from major flight corridors. But he added: “there will be a reevaluation of when we do this work.” 

The timing contrasts with how L3Harris describes its own method. In an interview published in March, Chris Collings, the L3Harris vice president who runs the business, said the company never switches network segments off. At critical sites with two paths, he said, crews upgrade one path, validate it, then upgrade the other, during low-traffic windows. The network is designed to contain a local fault, so why one remote radio site could disrupt most of the country’s en route centers remains unexplained.

Duffy repeatedly blamed the contractor. “We’re going to hold people accountable,” he said, adding that many contractors “take our money and provide really poor service.” He also told reporters he was “stuck with L3Harris.” 

In a statement, L3Harris said it was supporting the agency’s investigation, and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The FAA said that one of its representatives helped an L3Harris technician gain access to an agency site on Friday. The union for FAA technicians, however, said its members had no part in the work. Historically, it said in a statement Saturday, contractors have relied on FAA employees to assess risk and coordinate maintenance, but its “technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.” 

The FAA has acknowledged that its technician workforce is understaffed and released a workforce plan in May 2026 calling for an increase of at least 750 more certified technicians by 2030. “However, little progress has been made on hiring those new technicians,” the union said. The FAA and L3Harris did not respond to a series of emailed questions for this story.

A push to shift from L3Harris to AT&T

L3Harris, based in Melbourne, Fla., specializes in defense, but it has run the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, known as FTI, since its predecessor Harris Corp. won the contract in 2002. The company says it has already converted 70% of the copper-to-fiber conversion. 

The agency has had warnings about the network for years, including a failure strikingly like Friday’s. On Nov. 19, 2009, an FTI outage hit 129 air traffic facilities. The inspector general concluded that configuration and procedural errors by Harris caused the outage and delayed restoring service. A Harris engineer had put a new router into service in Los Angeles that carried a configuration error. Even after fixes, the inspector general noted, FAA and Harris officials acknowledged a continuing risk of critical outages.

The FAA has since faulted the company publicly. After a September 2025 telecom outage at the Dallas approach-control facility halted flights at both of the city’s major airports for hours, the agency blamed failures in service from local carrier Frontier Communications. It added: “Oversight by L3Harris, an FAA contractor, failed to ensure that redundancies in the system functioned properly.” L3Harris responded that it and the carriers had warned the FAA for years that the circuits needed replacing, but the money never came.

This September, a primary circuit serving the Philadelphia approach-control facility failed, and after L3Harris advised switching to a backup fiber line, which turned out to have been cut by a construction crew in New Jersey. About 9,500 U.S. flights were delayed or canceled. “When it fails, we just don’t have the redundancy” of a modern architecture, Bedford said at the time.

The FAA is already moving to replace FTI. In August, using waiver authority tied to the modernization program, it made a single, undefinitized award to AT&T to lead the FAA Enterprise Network Services program, FTI’s successor. The award started with a $74.3 million task order for what the FAA expects to be a multibillion-dollar contract lasting up to 15 years. In September, Bedford called for an additional $10.5 billion from Congress for the project. On Saturday, Duffy said that Verizon and Lumen were also “ready to go” on the upgrade. Until that transition is done, L3Harris remains the operator, and the contractor converting the FAA’s copper lines.

The FAA network is a small part of a company that has become more central to the administration’s priorities. L3Harris, which reported $21.9 billion in revenue last year, converted a Boeing 747 donated by Qatar into an interim Air Force One this year. It worked against a July 4 deadline that, Democratic senators say, forced it to scale back the usual upgrade package. (The Air Force has said the work would cost less than $400 million; the contract is classified.) 

In January, the Pentagon agreed to invest $1 billion in L3Harris’s missile business, which the company plans to spin off—a rare direct federal stake in a major defense supplier. And in July, the Space Force awarded L3Harris up to $955 million to build 18 missile-defense satellites for the Golden Dome shield, bringing its orders for U.S. missile-tracking and defense satellites to at least 70.

What the GAO found about the FAA upgrade

The GAO’s September report examined the FAA’s upgrade. Of the $12.5 billion Congress allocated, $9 billion is for systems modernization. Telecommunications is one of 13 programs in the overhaul’s first phase: replacing 5,170 copper lines with fiber and moving nearly 30,000 services to Internet Protocol. GAO figures show the program’s estimated cost rising from about $4.75 billion to about $5.91 billion. 

The auditors’ main findings:

  • There’s no reliable cost estimate. In June the FAA put phase one’s systems work at $10.6 billion, but officials could not produce the analysis behind the figure, telling auditors it would take a tremendous effort to find. The estimate omits government costs, most operating and maintenance costs and all of phase two. The FAA says it needs another $10.8 billion.
  • There’s no master schedule. Peraton, the prime systems integrator, delivered a preliminary integrated master schedule in April. As of May, though, the 11,389 project schedules had not been integrated, which risked inefficiencies and conflicts with airport operations. Officials said loading them all into their scheduling tool “would not be useful or helpful.” The FAA planned to use an artificial intelligence tool to flag conflicts, but as of May it was still being tested and rules for using it had not been set.
  • Rules were waived. In August 2025, Bedford issued a blanket waiver exempting the program from nearly all of the FAA’s acquisition management requirements, including the one that would require a lifecycle cost estimate. The GAO called that a key reason no such estimate exists.

The Transportation Department partly agreed with the GAO’s two recommendations: build a reliable lifecycle cost estimate and a detailed integrated master schedule. In its reply, the department said 12 of 13 workstreams, covering over 95 percent of project tasks, were on plan as of July. According to the FAA’s public Modern Skies dashboard, 11 out of 12 programs are at or ahead of plan. The exception is the replacement of analog protocol converters, devices that turn analog signals into digital ones, which stands at 8 percent complete, with just 45 of 69 planned sites completed in the most recent month recorded. 

The FAA has said it will answer the GAO’s September recommendations in detail within 180 days of the report, a deadline that falls in March.

Whose upgrade was it?

Bedford tried to separate Friday’s failure from the modernization program. “We’re conflating modernization with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend $1 billion a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980s [legacy] telco network,” Bedford said. “This is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort.”

That contrasts with the GAO’s account, which lists the copper-to-fiber program as part of phase one of the modernization. And according to the GAO, existing program contracts were modified to give Peraton authority to manage the other contractors on the FAA’s behalf. “Peraton, think of them as an extension of me,” Bedford said in April. 

Peraton was seen as an underdog for the FAA job, in part because it had little prior experience working with the agency. The company itself grew out of the government IT services unit of Harris Corp., L3Harris’ predecessor, which private equity firm Veritas Capital bought and rebranded as Peraton in 2017. 

Before the FAA award, agency staff had rated the company a high risk for financial instability in an October 2025 presentation to Duffy, Bloomberg reported in September. When agency staff evaluated the bids last year, they graded Peraton and Parsons, which bid alongside IBM, on four technical criteria, according to the presentation. Parsons rated better on three and the same on the fourth. Staff wrote that Peraton’s answers to use cases and direct questions “often focused on matters irrelevant to the discussion topic.”

Peraton scored better on past performance, helped by a positive review from NASA. The FAA told Bloomberg that strong ratings from Peraton’s customers, including NASA, were among its reasons for the choice, along with what it called the company’s significant telecommunications experience. The presentation also showed that Peraton sought a higher award fee than Parsons; it is unclear whether that changed later in the process.

Politico reported in June that a former Duffy spokesperson, Mark Bednar, who now sits on the board of the nonprofit that paid for Duffy’s road-trip video series, Great American Road Trip Inc., had lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. At a December 2025 congressional hearing, Bedford said career FAA staff ran the selection without interference from Duffy or Trump. The recommendation went from Bedford to Duffy and then to the president, he said, and Trump demanded a $200 million cut in the fee.

Concerns about Peraton’s work have since dogged the program. A few months ago, the FAA called Peraton in and told it to improve its performance, and the company blamed the agency in return, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The FAA has said it hasn’t penalized Peraton or issued the company a formal warning about poor performance.

A Peraton spokesperson told Bloomberg in August that the program is on track. But the company said the schedule is among the largest and most complex in government history, covering 330,000 independent projects and half a million dependencies. Peraton did not respond to an inquiry for this story. 

Duffy used the outage to renew and even scale up his call for Congress to fund the larger telecom modernization effort, arguing the $12.5 billion already allocated is not enough. For weeks, he has been calling for $30 billion in additional funds—with only about $10 billion of that request specifically for air traffic modernization—but during the outage he raised the demand to $50 billion. Bedford said the FAA would review its upgrade protocols. Neither said whether copper-to-fiber cutovers would be paused while investigators work out why and how one router could halt the country’s air traffic.

Representative James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight Committee, said on Saturday that Duffy must be questioned by Congress, including about why the work was being conducted “on a busy travel day, as opposed to in the middle of the night where a disruption wouldn’t have been so damaging because they’re rushing.”

#10417. No, the Pixel Tag is not available today

Our first impressions on Google’s new Pixel Tag are live, but orders are not. There appears to be some confusion running around the web, but the Pixel Tag is not available for purchase today.

Update 11/11: Right on schedule, Google has opened up Pixel Tag sales through the Google Store and Amazon.

Announced in August, the Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker directly from Google, and it’s been worth the wait. In our initial review earlier today, we found it to be a solid option with polish not found on third-party alternatives. It doesn’t magically make Find Hub a perfect tracking network, but it’s as good as it gets, at least based on our brief experience so far.

But the Pixel Tag isn’t available to buy just yet.

I think (at least for me) part of the confusion is from Damien's review video that is/was featured on the site... He says the Pixel Tag is available to be purchased right now within the first few seconds of the video. And mentioned it again that you can buy them today later on.

Rather, the official Pixel Tag release date is November 11. As it stands today, the Google Store is not accepting orders, nor are any third-party retailers that you may have seen linked in posts around Pixel Tag availability today. Pricing is still set for $29.99 for a 1-pack and $99.99 for a 4-pack.

Google explicitly said in a blog post just this morning:

Pixel Tag offers peace of mind so you always know where your most important things are — and it’s available November 11.

We’re eager to get our hands on more of these trackers too, but we’ve got just a bit longer to wait.

#10416. Today’s leaders. Tomorrow’s bad role models?

There is a rising generation of students in high school and college who are forming beliefs about how to lead. The most prominent examples of leaders in politics, business, and education make me concerned about the future.

Role models are an important part of the way we learn how a complex task should be handled. We may adopt the behaviors of role models or react against them, but we internalize a lot of the prominent people around us. I’ll highlight a few of the problems I see and explore some potential solutions.

The negative role models

Politics has been the source of negative role models for future leaders for a long time. For decades, politicians being interviewed on television repeated talking points that were only vaguely related to the questions they were asked. The support of leaders for issues often depended more on party affiliation than on whether the position would lead to a meaningful benefit. And over the past 10 years, there has been a rise in true mean-spirited rhetoric that has devolved into name calling and insults rather than reasoned discussions of the issues of the day.

The last decade has had few inspiring business leaders either. Prominent news stories focus on billionaires who are chasing additional profits while currying favor with leaders who have political power. The heads of AI companies forge ahead with the development of models that require resource-intensive data centers without letting concerns about the economic, social, and environmental costs of the work influence the pace of development of new models.

University leaders have generally been no better. Many universities around the country have become highly politicized. Some university leaders are so paralyzed by the politics around them that they refuse to make any changes at all. Others push forward changes without bringing the community along with them to achieve their ends and alienate their students, staff, and faculty in the process.

None of these are examples of healthy leadership.

What is healthy leadership?

Ultimately, good leadership involves three key components. Leaders must establish a vision for the future that brings people along with them and inspires them to engage to create that future. Leaders must grapple with the complexity of the world and work to develop solutions to significant problems that chart a course through competing priorities. Finally, leaders must meet the moment in a principled way in which they communicate clearly about the factors that drive the path forward.

In politics, one of the differences between campaigning and governing is that campaigns can be one based on emphasizing the negatives of an opponent, while governing requires supporting a course of action that addresses key problems. In an era of perpetual campaigning, it can be difficult to find people who actually embrace a position and see it through.

In all aspects of life, there are rarely courses of action that are good for everyone all the time. Instead, everything has tradeoffs. Great leaders recognize those tradeoffs, find a reasonable compromise among them, and then help the people they lead to recognize the value of that particular path. They are also committed to continuous improvement of outcomes even after they implement a change.

The path forward

To ensure that we have great leaders in the future, we have to acknowledge the absence of great role models at present. Then, there are two significant things we must do.

First, we must hold our leaders accountable to be better role models. That should start with our university leaders who are all educators at heart. They must take a step back from the local politics of their position and remember that their actions are being watched and may ultimately be emulated by others. We should also remind our business and political leaders that winning is important, but how you win also matters. Encourage them to do things that send the right message to the people learning from their example.

And those of us who teach and write about leadership must also provide a counterweight to the existing role models. If there are key skills that leaders should have that are not easily found among role models, then we must use them as examples of what not to do. We must point out ways that the short-term benefits of poor leadership have long-term negative consequences. As complex as the current moment may seem, the world of the future will be more complicated as the influences of climate change, globalization, artificial intelligence (and a host of other issues) affect the world. We will need leaders who unite us around a vision and take a far different approach than the leaders who dominate the news cycle right now.

#10414. 3 ways to calm your critical inner voice

My ride to work used to be a big red London bus. I’d hop on and head to Broadcasting House, the BBC headquarters near Oxford Circus. Along for the ride was my invisible companion: Negative Nancy.

She would pipe up: “Oh, off to Broadcasting House, are you? What are you going in there for? You don’t belong there.”

By this point I’d worked my way from a secretarial job to producer on a national personal finance show. I had every right to be proud of my success, but Nancy wouldn’t shut up.

She followed me into the office: “You look like you know what you’re doing, but you don’t.”

Then into the studio, where I’d be interviewing a politician: “Your questions aren’t very good.”

Thanks, Nancy. Any other helpful observations?

I was doing the job, but that commentary made it hard to enjoy anything I’d achieved.

We all have an inner voice. It’s the running conversation we have with ourselves, helping us make sense of the world without saying everything out loud. 

“It looks cold. Better take a coat.” Useful.

“You’re going to make a fool of yourself in that meeting.” Less useful.

When that voice turns negative, it can take up enormous headspace. Mine invalidated my hard work and success. It also thwarted my thoughts about career progression. At work, it can persuade perfectly capable people to keep an idea to themselves, avoid a difficult conversation, or let an opportunity pass. Self-doubt becomes the name of the game.

If you lead or support colleagues, you’ll recognize some of those behaviors. You may recognize the voice yourself.

ACE your self talk 

I use a simple acronym to help: ACE. Acknowledge, Choose, and Evidence. Three ways to turn down that negative commentary and make room for confident supporting voices.

1. Acknowledge the voice

First, I had to acknowledge there was in fact a voice inside my head. And acknowledge that the commentary, although familiar, wasn’t always factually accurate. 

Giving it a name helped me catch it in the act. “Oh, hello, Negative Nancy. You again.” You might have a Bring-Me-Down Brian or a Run-Me-Around Rita. Name yours whatever you like. 

The point is to recognize when that voice starts chipping away at your confidence.

Notice when it gets chatty, too. Before a meeting? When you’re trying something new? When an email from your boss arrives and you immediately think, “What have I done wrong?”

Once you are aware of it, you can start questioning it.

2. Choose not to listen

Nancy had plenty of opinions about my career, but I didn’t have to let her make the decisions.

“Thanks, Nancy, but I’m going into work now. I’ve got a show to produce. Get off the bus!”

It sounds a little ridiculous, having an argument with an imaginary passenger. But answering back helped me interrupt the commentary rather than let it run all day.

You can hear a doubtful thought and still choose to speak in the meeting, put yourself forward, or have that conversation. You don’t have to wait for Nancy’s permission.

And if the voice pops back up? Recognize it and choose to ignore it again. This takes practice.

3. Evidence: Remind yourself of the facts

Negative Nancy has a very selective memory. That awkward comment from five years ago? Perfect recall. All the good feedback since? Apparently, the files have gone missing.

So gather some evidence. What have you achieved? What have people trusted you to do? What experience are you bringing to this situation?

In my case, I’d worked my way up to producing a national radio show. I hadn’t wandered into Broadcasting House and found an unattended desk. People had employed me to do that job.

Keep a “brag book,” a notebook or folder where you save positive feedback, successful projects, and things you’re proud of. When your inner voice starts dismissing your ability, you’ll have something concrete to refer to.

You can help colleagues do this too. Remind them specifically what they did well and the difference it made. Give them something their Nancy will struggle to argue with.

Keep fighting the voice

I’m sorry to tell you this, but there’s no way to completely get rid of your mean inner monologue. Negative Nancy’s voice still occasionally pipes up for me—and I coach people on workplace confidence!

It’s in our nature. It kept us safe when we were cave dwellers (“Don’t leave the cave! There’s a saber-toothed tiger outside, you idiot!”) so it’s always going to be ready to pop up when we least want it to. 

But the more conscious we are of our pesky critical inner voice, the more we talk openly about it with our colleagues, the easier it becomes to question and quiet it.

#10413. Holiday gift guide 2026: 20 thoughtfully curated tech gifts that will charm and delight everyone on your list

As the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating. But that’s not to say that there aren’t options out there. I often find that the best gifts are charming, focused devices with a touch of style. 

My selection process for this gift guide was entirely subjective. Almost everything on it is a gadget or design object with an element of tactile satisfaction for how it handles an everyday task. You won’t find a boring black rectangle anywhere on the list, and you shouldn’t have to think too hard about the soaring cost of memory.

Apple: The First 50 Years by David Pogue

Published to mark Apple’s half-century this year, veteran tech journalist David Pogue has marked the occasion with a hefty tome that serves as a biography of the company itself. Pogue conducted 150 interviews for the book, including figures like Jony Ive and Steve Wozniak, and the presentation benefits from hundreds of photos throughout. This is a book that’s worth owning in print.

Twelve South Airfly SE

Some airplane seatback screens support Bluetooth, but it’s not something you can always rely on when boarding a long-haul flight, as many screens still won’t connect to noise-canceling headphones. Twelve South’s AirFly SE is an inexpensive dongle that plugs into your seat’s headphone jack and transmits the audio to your cans. You’ll never need to use airline earbuds again.

Sharge Flow Mini Go

Sharge’s whole thing is designing utilitarian gadgets with a stylish twist, and the Flow Mini Go is one I can recommend to anyone who ever finds themselves running low on a charge. It has a 5,800-milliampere-hour (mAh) battery, 22.5-watt charging and a built-in cable, as well as an option to attach it directly to your phone’s USB-C port. Just as importantly, it’s only about as big as a lipstick tube. 

Nothing Ear (a)

At $79, Nothing’s Ear (a) model is my pick for affordable wireless earbuds. They sound great and look even better, especially if you opt for the construction-equipment-yellow pair. Even the charging case is cool, with a design inspired by medicinal blister packs.

Logitech MX Master 4 Developer Edition

If you know someone who uses a mouse all day but has never really thought about the actual mouse they’re using, the MX Master 4 might just change their life. The MX Master series has long been considered the leading productivity mouse due to its unique free-spinning scroll wheel, and the latest model adds a customizable haptic thumb panel that buzzes to confirm a shortcut. The new Developer Edition adds a “Hello, World” prompt and a reference to the Linux kernel’s release date.

BOOX Palma 3

The Boox Palma 3 is an E Ink reader the size and shape of a smartphone, offering a convenient antidote to doomscrolling that you can take anywhere. Because it runs on Android, you can easily add your Kindle and Kobo libraries straight from the Google Play store. This latest version features a streamlined aluminum design and stylus support.

8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard

8BitDo is best known for its excellent range of gaming controllers, and its first mechanical keyboard turned out to be just as haptically satisfying. Launched in versions that evoked the Nintendo Entertainment System and the Famicom, the lineup now includes models inspired by the Commodore 64 and the IBM Model M.. Each comes with enormous programmable buttons you can place next to the keyboard, making copying and pasting feel like a session at the arcade.

Balmuda The Lantern

Balmuda is a hip Japanese appliance maker best known for its minimalist steam toaster, but its equally obsessive take on the camping lantern may be a more practical gift. It has a single rotary dial that takes you from a warm, flickering candle-style effect at the low end to a brighter reading light when you turn it up. The light is diffused through a pipe for a soft glow, and its rechargeable battery means you can use it anywhere from the bedroom to the balcony.

Analogue Pocket

The Analogue Pocket feels like it came from an alternate universe where Apple designed the Game Boy. It has a gorgeous stripped-down design, an amazing high-resolution screen, and programmable hardware that has been tuned to provide the most authentic reproduction possible of Game Boy and Game Boy Advance games. The newer Analogue 3D does much the same thing for the Nintendo 64, if your gift recipient is more of a couch potato.

Lego Game Boy

Lego’s Game Boy is another meticulous reproduction of the Game Boy, but from a totally different angle. This kit is incredibly fun to build, making you build up the hardware from the circuit board level and work on the mechanisms of the satisfyingly squishy buttons and D-pad. As a display piece, you can swap out cartridges and lenticular screen inserts for Super Mario Land and The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening.

Backbone One

The BackBone One has been around for a while, but together with its Pro version, it still remains the top name in smartphone game controllers. And the proposition is more compelling than it used to be, with modern phones now powerful enough to run solid versions of high-end console games like Assassin’s Creed Mirage and Death Stranding. Backbone offers models with both PlayStation and Xbox controller layouts, depending on your preference.

Aura Carver Mat

Digital photo frames have been a clichéd throwaway gift for a long time, which is why Aura’s products stand out. The Carver Mat is a landscape, color-calibrated matte screen with a paper-textured border that automatically dims its lighting to match the ambient surroundings, making it feel much more natural than other digital frames. It can display two portrait photos side-by-side and even supports Live Photos from an iPhone. 

Kodak Charmera

The Kodak Charmera hits on two recent trends: Labubu-style blind-box collectibles and the throwback use of lo-fi digicams. Each $35 box contains one of seven retro designs, and the tiny camera itself has several filters and frames. The image quality is not great, of course, but the Charmera is well-designed and well-named—it’s the perfect stocking stuffer.

Fujifilm Instax Pal 2

If you like the idea of a tiny pocket camera but want the results to be a little more usable, Fujifilm has you covered with the $169 Instax Pal 2. It’s shaped like a vintage range finder, like many of Fujifilm’s more advanced mirrorless cameras—but even though it fits in the palm of your hand, it makes room for an optical viewfinder, a 1-inch display, a command dial for color effects, and a lever to swap between aspect ratios. Photos can be transferred directly to your phone or to an Instax Link printer.

Peak Design Mobile Tripod

The biggest problem with tripods is finding a way to take them with you. But here’s one you won’t even notice in your jeans pocket. Peak Design’s take on the mobile tripod folds three legs and a full-on ball head into a package that’s about 5 millimeters thick. It snaps onto your MagSafe-compatible phone with minimal obtrusion, and unfolds into a stand you can angle for group shots, video calls, or hyper-lapses.

Native Union Pop cables and phone

I’ve long been a fan of Paris-based Native Union, which puts out some of the most thoughtfully designed tech accessories around. Its coiled Pop Cables are particularly great, avoiding tangles and saving desk space—and now the company has revived its original Pop Phone, giving you an old-school handset to conduct your Zoom calls like you’re in an episode of Mad Men. There’s even a hang-up button.

Xiaomi Portable Electric Air Compressor

If you know anyone who rides a bicycle and plays basketball, this gadget might just change their life. For everyone else, it’s still worth keeping around—I’ve recommended it to countless friends. This USB-C-powered air compressor has modes tailored to all sorts of devices and displays the real-time pressure rating on its LCD screen.

Nintendo Sound Clock: Alarmo

Trust Nintendo to come up with a bizarrely useful take on something as mundane as the alarm clock. Anyone who shares a bed with a partner may consider it a hard sell to start each morning with sounds from Mario Kart or The Legend of Zelda. But the motion-sensing feature alone is a game changer for the groggy moments before getting up; the screen stays switched off until you turn your head to check the time.

Teenage Engineering Pocket Operator

Swedish design company Teenage Engineering first made its name through its iconoclastic synthesizers, and it sounds like the company might be moving on from that heritage. If that’s the case, now could be a good time to stock up on its $99 Pocket Operator series. It’s a range of exposed circuit boards with clicky switches, rotary dials, and monochrome LCD panels, all amounting to remarkably capable instruments.

Yukai Engineering Nekojita FuFu

In Japan, if you’re sensitive to hot food or liquids, you’re said to have a nekojita—in other words, a cat’s tongue. Yukai Engineering is attempting to solve this condition with a tiny, rechargeable cat that attaches to the rim of your coffee cup or ramen bowl. Its internal fan drops the liquid’s temperature to a drinkable level in just a few minutes, and the cat looks cute in the process.

#10412. I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

Unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

It’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without issue. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

It does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

Because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

The Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

On the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only issue I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

The homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

The buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

It’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

As far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.
