#10410. The probable future is bleak. It’s time for improbable futures

Massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain. A crowd marches on the Interior Ministry and is driven back with bayonets. Students tear their school apart and barricade the doors; after hours of fighting with police, the army is called in.

This is Paris in March 1883, and it bears striking similarities to Paris in October 2026, when grievance became a national movement. Then, it was about bread and work; today, the cost of living and declining public services. Then, the industrial revolution added a backdrop of anxiety; today, another revolution in technology. Then, as now, students rebelled against the schools meant to form them. 

France is an extreme case of a global mood. Across the 30 countries tracked by Ipsos, the public opinion research firm, 62% say their country is on the wrong track. In the U.S., the figure is 73%; in France, it’s 89%. Edelman, a communications consultancy, finds in its annual trust survey that only 32% of people across 28 countries expect the next generation to be better off. In the U.S., it’s 21%, and in France it’s just 6%. These numbers are so bad that the social contract, that bedrock of civil society, is at risk. 

The problem isn’t a lack of change. It’s that the change underway isn’t the change people want.

If the probable future is bleak, the most pragmatic thing to do is to take seriously the quest for improbable futures. Unfortunately, that is not a muscle most political or business leaders have built, trained as they are in playing the present game, not inventing entirely new forms of social and financial value. The case study method of business schools entrenches lessons from the past, not from the future; being trained in the logic of the law and finance does not naturally foster the kind of empathetic creativity that designs for what people want next. 

You can see it at this time of year, as companies draw up their annual plans: new columns in spreadsheets unwittingly determining a future that’s very much like the past, plus a bit. This year many companies will bake artificial intelligence into their forecasts to drive efficiency: a future that’s very much like the past, minus a bit. Is that really our highest aspiration for what people claim to be the most powerful technology ever created? And there is growing evidence that AI may deepen the problem. It favors the incremental over the radically new, making everyone’s ideas more alike.

The probable future is not destiny

The probable future is just one scenario among many. If we make different choices, we can design for something different: a plausible future, or more ambitiously, a possible future—or even, if we really allow ourselves to dream—a preposterous future. The field of strategic foresight describes this as the “futures cone.” Designed and built well, ambitious ideas start in the outer bounds, moving towards the center with diligent work. 

In 1956, Britain’s Astronomer Royal called space travel “utter bilge.” A moon landing became possible when the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth in 1961, plausible when John F. Kennedy put the weight of the U.S. government behind it, and probable when Apollo 10’s dress rehearsal succeeded in May 1969. One of humanity’s defining acts went from “bilge” to history in 13 years.

History does not give us a road map to what’s next, but it does suggest some principles as to how to pursue the improbable.

1: Respond to a crisis with creativity

While good times encourage incrementalism, the toughest moments open receptivity for the bold. The economist Milton Friedman went so far as to say that only a crisis produces real change, and that when it comes, “the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around.” The fragility of these moments can lead to great damage, or great progress. The Red Cross was inspired by the ravages of war. So were the Bauhaus, the German architecture and design movement, and the Paralympics. Today’s pervasive discontent does not preclude ambitious ideas; it creates the context for creation. 

2: Take the first steps towards a preferable future

The Schuman Declaration of 1950 proposed cooperation between France and West Germany for coal and steel. Two countries, two products. The aim was to make war between them “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” A united Europe was preposterous just five years after World War II, but as the declaration put it, “Europe will not be made all at once, or according to a single plan.” That first, discrete partnership began the process of bringing the preposterous towards the plausible.

3: Be willing to look ridiculous, together

The most important principle is psychological. By their nature, improbable ideas are early, may be wrong, and risk ridicule. A prominent professor of futures studies, Jim Dator, in his second law of the future, goes so far as to say that any useful idea about the future should appear to be ridiculous. Which means its champions must be willing to be ridiculed. This is not natural in the meeting rooms, PowerPoint presentations and three-year plans where the future is articulated. 

It helps to assemble a group of people to withstand this phase. The 12 men who met in a London print shop in 1787 to end Britain’s slave trade had each other, and soon took their cause across England with lecture tours and petitions. This is where language, symbols, and rituals come in: visible signs of belonging and strength in numbers. The abolitionists had their Wedgwood medallion, with its image of a Black man in chains and its unforgettable motto, “Am I not a man and a brother?” The Red Cross had its emblem. From chants to T-shirts to lapel pins, the champions of the improbable need to see and find each other. 

What happened after the 1883 Parisian protests?

While many of the French protestors of 1883 were expelled from school and others arrested, that same year, a 20-year-old of no great achievements, troubled by a nation still reeling from its defeat by Prussia, asked himself how he could help foster the character of a generation, such that civil society could thrive. He traveled across the Channel to England, home to the industrial revolution and an empire, and began researching its education system. He decided that playing sports was central to England’s development of citizens. It was where they learned respect, fair play, and collaboration within the context of rules. 

After nearly a decade of study and campaigning, this man stood up at the Sorbonne—just steps from the school the students had barricaded—and closed a speech by proposing the revival of the Olympic Games, dormant for some 1,500 years. The audience applauded, but almost nothing happened. 

The idea of uniting the world around sport was preposterous. So he took the first steps. In 1894, he slipped the Olympic revival onto the agenda of a congress on amateur sport. He convened 78 delegates, formed a 13-member International Olympic Committee, publicly declared their intent, invited others in, and championed the language and symbols of grand, shared endeavor. Within four years of his first sharing his preposterous, idealistic, pro-human idea, the first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896. 

The young man was Pierre de Coubertin, and he set in motion humanity’s greatest gathering, which draws billions of people into shared drama and values, from a moment of crisis much like our own. 

So for anyone drawing up next year’s plan, know that the gravitational pull towards the smart, expected future is strong. Ask yourself if there’s at least one possible, or even preposterous, idea on the table, how to take the first steps towards it, and who is going to hold the vision with you while it sounds absurd.

The world is looking for new ways forward. What’s our de Coubertin moment?

Sebastian Buck is a cofounder of ENSO, a future design company.

#10409. FEMA has a cord-cutting problem

On Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite shows interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS). The test will cut into live broadcasts and cable reruns alike, and also be heard on radio stations across the country. However, anyone getting their TV fix from Netflix, Disney+, or any other streaming service likely won’t notice a thing.

That’s bad news, especially when the next real emergency happens. According to recent Nielsen data, U.S. consumers are already spending half their TV viewing time with digital video platforms like YouTube and Amazon Prime. In other words: Half of America’s TV viewers are missing out on emergency alerts because they’re watching online instead.

“It is vital that emergency alert systems adapt to changes in consumer technologies,” says University of Colorado Denver communications professor Hamilton Bean, an expert in public alert and warning systems. “Whether through streaming services, mobile devices, or IoT [Internet of Things], emergency alerts work best when they reach people where they are—at home, at work, or in public settings.”

The federal government first began testing emergency alerts in the 1950s to warn citizens of a possible Soviet nuclear attack. Federal alert systems have been modernized multiple times since those early days, including an expansion to mobile phones in 2012. But in recent years, regulators and emergency management officials have struggled to keep up with rapidly changing media consumption habits and shifts in the TV business.

This has led to confusing gaps in the Emergency Alert System. One example: Consumers who have switched their TV subscriptions from a cable company to an internet-based TV service like YouTube TV, Fubo, or Hulu + Live TV may also miss out on alerts. These so-called “virtual” pay TV operators don’t participate in the EAS, which means they don’t interrupt their programming to carry such warnings.

But if a YouTube TV subscriber happens to be tuned into a local broadcast network like ABC or Fox, they may see the alert after all. Those channels are frequently ingested from local broadcast TV affiliates, which in turn do work with FEMA. In other words: YouTube TV subscribers who watch Dancing With the Stars on ABC during an emergency may get a warning, while those tuned into Bravo’s Southern Charm may be blissfully unaware of any impending danger.

“Regardless of the other aspects of regulation, when it comes to public safety issues, [traditional and internet-based pay TV services] should be on equal footing,” says John Bergmayer, legal director of the nonprofit technology advocacy group Public Knowledge. Virtual pay TV services already need to know a subscriber’s location to serve up local broadcast channels, which should help them target consumers with the right alerts. “And like cable, they have the technical capacity to both interrupt a program or to add some sort of crawl along the bottom of the screen,” Bergmayer says.

Streaming services and their media company owners have generally resisted the idea of being forced to carry emergency alerts. In a 2021 regulatory filing, the Motion Picture Association, which counts Netflix, Disney, and Skydance among its members, declared that it would be “enormously technically difficult, if not entirely impracticable” to expand emergency alerts to streaming.

One problem the industry association pointed to is the federated nature of America’s Emergency Alert System. While Tuesday’s test alert goes out nationwide, real warnings about wildfires or flooding are necessarily local. Requiring a streaming service like Netflix to relay those alerts would mean building out extensive monitoring infrastructure in every state.

Some hope that the new Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) 3.0 broadcast standard, which brings modern technologies to antenna TV, will come to the rescue. In theory, modern TVs equipped with ATSC 3.0 tuners could interrupt a Netflix stream as soon as they receive an emergency alert via antenna. In practice, there’s no regulation in place to require this yet. Critics also fear that ATSC 3.0’s content protection technologies could hamper emergency warnings.

In the end, the lesson from Tuesday’s test may be that emergency alerts can’t rely on just one technology. “There is no silver bullet,” says Art Botterell, author of To Warn Is Human: A Cultural History of Public Warning. Instead of trying to find a tech fix, he’d prefer that we invest in civic infrastructure and strengthen the bonds between neighbors so they can alert and help one another. “We need to facilitate that person-to-person sharing,” Botterell says.

That, in turn, may also help people who happen to tune into the wrong TV show at the wrong moment.

#10406. The young rebel alliance trying to get people to love technology again

In a spare and cavernous former eyewear emporium near the luxury stores of San Francisco’s Union Square, a motley group of tech devices is spread out across display counters and pedestals. One is a desktop computer shaped like a cartoon frog. Another is an e-ink laptop controlled by buttons made of felt. Nearby, there’s an AI assistant hidden inside a fuzzy parrot meant to perch on a user’s shoulder.

The space is like some bizarro Apple Store, but instead of offering futuristic devices you didn’t know you needed, it’s a showcase of devices you didn’t know could even exist.

This store is not a store, but a three-year-old gallery called the Intersection of Art and Technology, or TIAT, which hosts a near-constant stream of events, meetups, and exhibitions focused on experimentation among self-described creative technologists. The devices are part of TIAT’s latest group exhibition, Every Thing Computer, which explores “playful computing” and experimental interfaces.

Some are clearly one-off art projects (see the punchable oversize keyboard escape button and the computer mouse shaped like female genitalia), but others are more earnest and commercial attempts to reimagine what we want our devices to be.

Many of the people showing at TIAT, who consider themselves both artists and technologists, are building these devices as physical proof that an alternative to the current Silicon Valley ecosystem is possible. They are part of a growing community in San Francisco and beyond reconsidering how technology can bring people more joy—or at least give them more agency over the devices they use.  

“We like to call this the rebel alliance of creatives that are trying to go out and have better ideas for what the future can be,” says Liz Dorman, whose San Francisco-based startup, Era, sponsored the exhibition at TIAT. Her company is building a platform for customizable AI devices, putting her near the center of the creative technologist ecosystem.

Thanks to AI tools, more nimble factories, and the motivation of a generation who grew up with smartphones in their hands, the prospect of developing new kinds of devices is more possible, and desirable, than ever before.

“We’ve had so much lock-in and walled-garden effects because of the App Store and because of how hard it is to make hardware,” Dorman says. “That now is finally changing.”

But taking down Big Tech is beside the point for many of the people in the creative technology community. Instead of competing at the same massive scale as the tech giants, these ambitious, and predominantly young, tech people are trying to build new hardware that both serves a niche audience and broadens the spectrum of consumer technology. The more commercial among these devices are just now starting to ship, and they’re meeting the market in a moment of highly anticipated AI hardware coming from companies with trillion-dollar valuations. 

“That’s precisely why we need artists to provide perspectives on all this new technology,” says Ash Herr, TIAT’s founder.

A DIY resurgence

While there are no hard numbers on how big this scene is, there are emerging and established creative technology groups and meetups from San Francisco to New York, including TIAT, Physical Futures, Fidget Camp, Gray Area, the School for Poetic Computation, the New Museum’s New Inc., the Resonant Computing Lab, and more. Many have academic roots in vaunted computing and human-computer interface labs like Carnegie Mellon’s Human-Computer Interaction Institute, New York University’s Interactive Telecommunications Program, and several labs at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

“There are a lot of students who are kind of tired of computers,” says Marcelo Coelho, director of MIT’s Design Intelligence Lab. “In many ways, their response is to invent their own computer.”

People exploring these concepts often self-describe as creative technologists, but some see their work more broadly as indie hardware, while others find it to be closer to fashion hardware or even bespoke “couture computing.” The through line is a desire to break out of the winner-takes-all mindset that’s fueled the Big Tech companies in recent years.

“Pretty much the story of San Francisco right now is all these people with egos being like, ‘I know what the future is. Let me tell you what the future is.’ And you can’t edit or change anything,” Dorman says. “A lot of the underlying stuff that’s happening in creative tech is coming from those feelings of we actually want to take ownership over our technology.”

Dorman describes this as a shift to “couture technology,” where a more open ecosystem would allow people to customize hardware to their own specific needs. “It’s like you can sew your own shirt, or you can buy it from your favorite creative, or you can get it mass-produced,” Dorman says.

Doing it yourself is nothing new for the modern tech world, of course. Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak built the earliest version of what would become an Apple computer in a bedroom. And it’s an ethos that’s carried through the years, according to Barry Threw, executive director of Gray Area, the San Francisco-based art and technology nonprofit that’s been leading tech-centered events, education, and research programs since 2008.

“Open hardware and people wanting to have some agency and access to these kinds of tools is always a trend that’s going on,” Threw says. He points to the mid-2010s, when there was a lot of interest in DIY hardware, through events like Maker Faire, and open-source software, printed circuit boards, and microcontrollers from Arduino and Raspberry Pi.

AI has opened new opportunities for this mode of creation, with vibe coding making it vastly easier to create digital tools and applications. “It makes it more attainable for folks who start doing interesting hardware and software DIY things because the software side of it doesn’t become such a burden,” Threw says.

But AI has also spurred a related backlash, as the leading AI labs and companies pursue advancements at a pace that has even some of its own executives worried for the future of humanity. As those few big companies appear to be guiding the direction of AI’s development, nearly three-quarters of people are concerned about what they are creating. 

“When people have less confidence in the direction of their public services and institutions, not just in tech but in general, I find this DIY ethos happening,” Threw says. “They go back to trying to take some agency into their own hands and build their own tools.”

In San Francisco and other tech hubs, the concern is also personal. Software engineers, once the backbone of Silicon Valley and the tech world at large, are finding themselves replaced by the very technology they once created, sparking existential crises about what, if anything, they can do next. Creative technology is proving to be one alternative.

“Across the technology spectrum, people are searching for where meaning and value and creativity lie when it’s not possible just to be a software engineer anymore because that stuff’s getting automated,” Threw says. “As the creativity around software development has been taken over by these AI tools, hardware is kind of the next frontier.”

Creating a new creative practice

Kelin Zhang holds up a camera and takes a photo of my face on her computer screen. We’re on a video call, the pandemic-cemented default meeting mode mediated through phones or laptops with built-in cameras. The camera she’s holding, though, is not some add-on element of another device. It’s a stand-alone camera meant for taking photos. But there’s a twist: Instead of actually producing a photo, the camera uses its lens to capture and process an image and then, for reasons that are not immediately apparent, uses AI to write and print a poem about it.

Poetry Camera is Zhang’s pet project turned consumer product. Conceived on a whim with her friend Ryan Mather back in January 2023, it was willed into being through a combination of online tutorials, AI vibe coding, open-source printed circuit boards, and 3D printers. After a weekend of poking around, they built a working prototype.

“I was like, wow, it’s a lot easier to get started in hardware than I thought,” she says.

Zhang wasn’t starting from scratch. She has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from MIT, and had spent nearly a decade working in digital product design. When she had the idea for Poetry Camera, she had just left her job as staff product designer at Twitter, which had recently been acquired by Elon Musk. “I got a front-row seat to everything and I thought, You know what? I’m kind of done with corporate tech,” she says. 

ChatGPT had been released publicly just a few months earlier, and Zhang had the sense that big changes were coming to the tech world. She decided to take a year to explore what it could look like to create an AI-first digital design practice. Poetry Camera was the first thing she prototyped.

“With AI, it’s only going to get easier and easier,” Zhang says. “If you’re motivated to work on a project, it lowers the barrier by so much.”

Almost four years later, Poetry Camera is a $349 consumer product that’s garnered fans in both the tech and poetry worlds. Anthropic, a longtime supporter, put in a rush order last winter for a batch to hand out at a Super Bowl party. Poetry Camera’s success has buoyed Zhang to start a physical product studio called Tenderworld. “People are excited and delighted by form factors that aren’t just apps trapped behind the screen of a phone or a computer,” she says.

Zhang picks up the Poetry Camera she used to take my photo and rips out the receipt-like thermal paper printed with the poem it created. But instead of focusing on my face on Zhang’s screen, the camera was looking past her laptop at a shelf of other Poetry Cameras in boxes. The poem it wrote was about itself.

‘Well, I want to change it’

Like a stall at a seedy flea market, there’s a table in a storefront window near San Francisco’s Transamerica Pyramid that’s covered with dozens of random consumer technology gadgets. Spanning the past five decades, they include a Macintosh Newton tablet, several varieties of early-2000s flip phones, an alien-esque cassette tape player, an AM/FM radio shaped like a peanut M&M, and multiple garish wristwatches with built-in cameras. Nestled among these are newer devices, like the Humane AI Pin and the Rabbit R1.

This display is part of the office of Era, the startup Dorman cofounded to build a software platform and hardware for customizable AI devices. None of the items on the table are for sale—this being San Francisco, people do pop in and ask—but rather they’re a nostalgia-tickling reminder that tech devices used to look a lot different from the rectangular phones in our pockets today. The display is a subtle prod at the bland landscape of modern hardware.

Why can’t tech look like this again?

“It hasn’t felt very optimistic recently, especially with all the releases happening by Big Tech companies,” Dorman says inside Era’s office, two 3D printers humming in the background. “It feels like these companies are not only out of touch with people, but they’re forcing technology onto people that they don’t actually want.”

Era, which has raised more than $11 million in funding, was founded to offer people the chance to decide what they want their tech to look like and how it can function, starting with the development of a puck-like AI core that it sees as the open-source basis of highly customizable devices. Calling itself “a small Gen Z team raised with smartphones,” the company is mostly twentysomethings who were still in grade school when the first iPhone was released. Dorman, who grew up in New Jersey jailbreaking the early iPhone models, was dismayed when Apple made that kind of custom hacking impossible.

Later, after an internship at Apple, she got her own job in Big Tech working for Humane, the company cofounded by former Apple executive Imran Chaudhri that raised more than $230 million to create a post-iPhone screenless AI device. That device, the AI Pin, flopped, and Dorman was not surprised. The fact that its form factor so closely resembled a police officer’s body-worn camera was one major issue, but so were more aesthetic concerns. Dorman, for one, thought there should be more variety than the single black-and-white color palette, and more of an embrace of the flexibility AI offers.

“I hated the voice and personality we chose for the device. It was the equivalent of giving everyone an iPhone and being like, you can’t change the wallpaper. And I was like, ‘Well, I want to change it,’” she says. And she did, hacking her AI Pin to use the voice of the blogger-narrator from the television teen drama Gossip Girl. She started showing off the device to her friends, and using it much more often than before. “That is very much the feeling that we’re chasing at Era.”

Dorman cofounded Era in 2025, teaming up with two other young AI-leaning technologists who were similarly concerned about the direction Big Tech and AI companies were heading.

“I think something that’s really true across the consumer landscape is everybody feels left behind by AI,” Era cofounder Megan Gole says. She previously worked at venture capital firm Sutter Hill Ventures, which was involved in OpenAI’s acquisition of former Apple design chief Jony Ive’s AI hardware startup Io in 2025. Seeing how the tech establishment envisioned AI’s rollout into mainstream culture struck her as too limited.

“Our options right now are join or die. Keep up with the AI bus or be a Luddite and get off your phone,” Gole says. Era offered a third way, built more from the ground up. “We want people’s feedback, and we want to create this new world that you guys are the center of,” she says.

Era’s intent is to provide the building blocks that make it easier for people to harness AI in their own specific and bespoke ways, breaking free from reliance on a phone to mediate its usage. The company’s puck device is envisioned as the computer inside whatever device a user wants to make, with the ability to access more than 15 different AI models and an interface that can adapt it to whatever task a user might imagine.

“Your tools can feel more retro in the sense that you know what each one is for, you use it, each interaction is meant to end, and you put it away,” Gole says.

In the AI-enabled future Era’s cofounders envision, people get to determine what, precisely, their devices are supposed to do, whether it’s a fridge magnet that delivers French cooking lessons or an e-ink display that reacts to the double-tap of a button to display the current time in Canberra, Australia.

“It enables people’s individuality to exist within an AI world that makes a very smooth median of everyone,” Gole adds.

Make hardware weird again

A few blocks away from Era’s quirky gadget collection, a different kind of AI hardware is taking shape. The much-hyped AI device from OpenAI and Io is taking final form inside the studio of LoveFrom, Ive’s closely guarded design firm. My recently planned visit to the studio was scuttled because OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was stopping by later in the day, and “everything is out,” someone at the company told me.

With Ive’s Apple design prestige and OpenAI’s market-driving muscle, many believe the forthcoming device could be the zeitgeisty iPhone of the AI age. People have reportedly taken to flying drones over LoveFrom’s studios hoping to catch a glimpse of whatever it is through now-shaded skylights.

Others are skeptical there will be a next dominant device form factor like the iPhone, or that consumers even want one to emerge.

Sebastian Bidegain and Harry Isaac‘s company, Noware, is betting there will be a market—or many markets—for much more niche tech devices. Their first product is a 128-gigabyte USB data stick, but one encased in a jewelry-inspired enclosure and glammed out with a tiny screen for customizable low-res animations. Designed to be worn as a necklace or attached as a bag charm, it’s an unexpected and flamboyant take on the banal task of carrying and sharing digital files. 

“We wanted some of the electronics in our lives to be more expressive and playful and just weird,” Isaac says.

Noware garnered enough in presales to fund production of the first batch of the device, named Puff, and its founders have managed to climb the learning curve of working with tech and jewelry manufacturers in China to actually get it built. “It’s difficult to manufacture. And that is maybe part of the reason why another bigger company hasn’t done something like this,” Bidegain says. “But I think that’s part of what makes it really cool.”

Bidegain and Isaac see barriers lowering all around, from the technology they use to design and prototype devices to the factories’ increasing ability to manufacture smaller batches of products. “For most other products there’s a range of options, and I think technology is going to be the same,” Isaac says. “I just think that the field is opening up more now that it’s becoming more accessible, and we want to be one of those options.”

Mina Fahmi also sees potential in niche tech devices. His startup, Sandbar, is building a wearable AI ring for note-taking, which sounds not all that different from the AI pins, pendants, and charms coming out from companies like Meta, Plaud, and Friend. But Sandbar’s ring, called Stream, isn’t trying to record everything. Instead, Stream is intended to be used to record specific thoughts from its wearer, who pushes a small integrated button and then whispers those thoughts directly into the ring. 

“A lot of people want to remember things without pulling out their phone,” Fahmi says.

On a recent video call, he brings his Stream ring up to his mouth and begins whispering. It’s so quiet I can’t hear him through his computer’s microphone, yet the ring picks up every word he says. It’s a way of reducing what Fahmi calls the friction of using voice to interact with technology, especially for personal thoughts or sensitive subjects. Stream, with its highly attuned microphone, is meant specifically for people to quickly record what they have in mind as easily as possible.

It’s a use case that Fahmi admits is on the fringe. There are plenty of other AI tools for capturing and summarizing conversations and work meetings, he concedes, but says not enough of them are built to help people record their own thoughts, ideas, and reflections. “We started Sandbar because we believed we would need new interfaces to fully realize the potential of AI for expanding human expression,” he says.

“We’re not out here trying to sell a million units in year one,” Fahmi adds. “What’s been clear to us is that it’s more important to create a thing that people really get value out of than to litter the earth with electronics.”

Tech gets personal

Back at TIAT’s exhibition opening, where a harpist is putting away her instrument and a DJ is setting up her decks, the crowd is thickening. Ken Kocienda stands out, and not just because he’s multiple decades older than most of the people in the room. Kocienda is arguably a member of the tech establishment that many in the exhibition are trying to rebel against. As a principal software engineer at Apple, he helped make the first iPhones, and is credited with creating its infamous keyboard autocorrect. He was also the head of product engineering at Humane.

Kocienda’s at the exhibition to see what some of the younger generations are trying to do with their technology. As someone who’s been coding since the 1980s, he’s forever curious about where software and hardware will go next, and he’s working on his own project to improve AI-assisted software development. He sees AI as opening up the potential for new forms of technology, especially special-purpose devices that run counter to the indispensable multitool approach of the iPhone. 

“I think the more personal we make technology, the more willing people are going to be to integrate it into their lives,” he says.

But that doesn’t mean Kocienda is abandoning his iPhone. “Computing paradigms don’t go away,” he says, arguing that major developments in technology build on each other while also changing the role of previous innovations. He sees a time when personally specific devices are what we primarily use, while our phones stay mostly tucked in pockets or bags, more utility than tool. “Even mainframes are still in use today,” he says.

MIT’s Coelho, who has a few students with projects in the TIAT show, says this moment of technological advancement is opening the doors to a wide range of new products and companies. “I think there’s an opportunity for thousands of startups to come up in this space,” he says.

The form these new devices will take is hard to predict, but there may be some seeds of that future in the TIAT exhibition. For TIAT founder Ash Herr, the purpose of the space is to expose more people to these emerging ideas, and to have people from across the technology and arts spectrums cross-pollinate. “I want people who are all in on their full-time tech jobs and people who are more feral to come together, learn, laugh, and ideate,” she says.

What, if anything, comes out of that is unclear. But for the creative technologists in this growing movement, the time seems ripe for offering up something new, and the tools are in their hands.

#10404. Why Portugal’s No. 7 jersey will forever look different

The Portuguese Football Federation can’t retire superstar soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo’s No. 7 due to strict FIFA rules around player numbers. Instead, the team got creative and used a different font. A No. 7 with a cross stroke through it will be used on kits for players who wear the number from here on out.

Portugal’s Saturday game against Denmark was the team’s first since Ronaldo retired earlier this month. The entire team came out in “Ronaldo 7” jerseys with the old-style number before the match to pay tribute to the player who captained the team for 19 years. Then during the match, player Carlos Forbs wore the new cross-stroke 7 for the Portuguese national team.

“This is yet another way to immortalize the meaning of such a special number and honor the legacy it represents,” the team said in a statement.

Other professional teams and leagues retire numbers to honor legendary players. In 1997, MLB retired the No. 42 for Jackie Robinson, the league’s first Black player and a former National League MVP. The NHL retired 99 in 2000 for Wayne Gretzky, who still holds the league’s record for most career points. The NBA’s Chicago Bulls will never again have a 4, 10, 23, or 33 after retiring them for Jerry Sloan, Bob Love, Michael Jordan, and Scottie Pippen, respectively.

The international football body doesn’t give teams or players as much freedom with numbers during its tournaments, as each team has to use all consecutive numbers from 1 to 26 for their 26-person rosters. That meant that when Lionel Messi retired in October, the Argentine Football Association didn’t retire his No. 10, despite the fact that Claudio Tapia, AFA’s president, said in 2024 it would be retired.

Portugal’s solution is a clever, unconventional work-around. If you can’t change the number, at least change how the number looks. Fonts with alternative characters, or characters with multiple design variations, give designers flexibility to add optional elements like swashes, flairs, or cross strokes on characters like 7 and Z.

By adding a cross stroke to their 7, Portugal figured out how to honor a retired legend with a number they technically can’t retire.

#10403. How Text-to-Image AI Generators Work, and 5 Tools That Deliver Good Results

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Type “a lighthouse on a cliff at dusk, oil painting, warm light” into a text box, wait ten seconds, and a picture that never existed appears. It feels like magic, but it is a well-understood pipeline of language models, neural networks and a great deal of math. Knowing how that pipeline works makes you a better prompter, helps you diagnose bad results, and makes it easier to choose the right tool for a job.

This guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it. It then compares five tools that consistently produce good results, starting with Pollo AI, and finishes with a practical workflow, a troubleshooting table and an FAQ. Plans, credits and model versions change often, so confirm current details on each vendor’s site before you commit to a subscription.

Early image generators were mostly GANs, or generative adversarial networks. A GAN pits two networks against each other: a generator that produces images and a discriminator that tries to spot fakes. GANs could produce sharp faces and textures, but they were hard to train, often collapsed into repeating the same few outputs, and were poor at following free-form text.

A second line of research used autoregressive models, which generate an image piece by piece the way a language model generates words. These handled text prompts better but were slow at high resolution.

The shift came with diffusion models. Researchers showed that a network trained to reverse a gradual noising process could generate images with excellent quality and diversity, and that it was far more stable to train than a GAN. Combine that with text conditioning and a compressed image representation, and you get the systems behind most of today’s tools. Newer models increasingly swap the traditional convolutional network for transformers, but the core idea of iterative denoising is still the foundation.

Under the hood, mainstream generators combine three ideas: a way to understand text, a way to represent images compactly, and a way to generate them gradually. The sections below follow a prompt from keystroke to finished picture.

Neural networks cannot read words, so your prompt is first split into tokens, small chunks of text such as whole words or word fragments. A text encoder then converts those tokens into an embedding, a grid of numbers that captures meaning and context. Many systems use encoders trained jointly on images and their captions, so that the text “a red bicycle” and pictures of red bicycles end up close together in the same mathematical space. Some newer systems add a large language model to understand longer, more detailed instructions.

This is why wording matters. The encoder only sees what you wrote, and it has a limited capacity. A short, specific prompt produces a clear signal. A long, rambling one dilutes each instruction.

Instead of drawing on a blank canvas, the model begins with random static. The pattern of that static is controlled by a seed number. The same prompt with a different seed gives a different image, because it starts from different noise. If a tool lets you fix the seed, you can make results repeatable and change just one variable at a time.

During training, engineers take millions of real images and add noise to them in small steps until only static remains. The network is then trained to predict the noise that was added at each step, which teaches it to reverse the process. At generation time, the model applies that skill to pure noise, removing a little at each step. Because it has learned what real images look like, the “noise” it removes gradually reveals something that looks plausible.

Your text embedding is fed into the network through a mechanism called cross-attention. At each step, parts of the evolving image can “look at” relevant parts of the prompt and adjust accordingly. A region that will become a lighthouse attends to the word “lighthouse”. A region that will become the sky attends to “dusk”.

A setting called classifier-free guidance, often shown as guidance scale or prompt strength, controls how strongly each step is pulled toward the prompt. The model computes one prediction with the prompt and one without it, then exaggerates the difference. A low value gives the model freedom and often more natural, varied results. A high value follows the words more literally but can produce oversaturated, over-sharpened or distorted images.

Running diffusion directly on full-resolution pixels would be very expensive. The idea behind Stable Diffusion, known as latent diffusion, is to compress images into a much smaller latent representation using an autoencoder. Denoising happens in that compact space, and a decoder turns the final latent back into a full image. This is a major reason high-quality generation now runs in seconds on a cloud GPU instead of minutes.

The number of denoising steps and the scheduler, which decides how much noise to remove at each step, shape the speed and look of the result. More steps usually add detail up to a point, then give diminishing returns. Many tools hide these settings, but the trade-off is always the same: fewer steps are faster and cheaper, more steps can look more refined.

Most pipelines finish with an upscaler or refinement pass that sharpens detail and fixes small artifacts. Many tools also offer inpainting, which regenerates only a selected region, outpainting, which extends the canvas, and variations, which restart from a related image.

A generator can only produce what it has learned to represent. Models are trained on very large collections of images paired with captions, and the quality, diversity and licensing of that data affect both the output and the legal picture. Models trained on more photographs tend to produce convincing photorealism. Models tuned on illustration and concept art lean toward painterly looks.

This also explains a few behaviors. Common subjects look great because the model has seen thousands of examples. Rare or very specific subjects, such as an unusual machine part or a niche cultural item, often look generic or wrong. Biases in the data can show up as stereotypes, for example in how “a doctor” or “a CEO” is depicted, so it helps to describe the people and setting you actually want.

Understanding the process explains the familiar failures:

Pollo AI’s text to image AI is a browser-based generator built around a simple loop: write a prompt, pick a style, generate, and download. Its page highlights HD output and a wide range of looks, from photorealistic scenes to cute cartoons, anime, pencil sketches, isometric art, abstract compositions and surreal visuals. Files can be downloaded as WebP, PNG or JPEG, a practical spread for web work: WebP keeps pages light, PNG preserves clean edges and transparency-friendly graphics, and JPEG works almost everywhere.

Pollo is also part of a wider platform that covers AI video, so a still image you like can become the starting point for motion without switching ecosystems. That matters for teams producing social content, because one workflow can cover both the image and the short clip built from it.

Things to check: the page does not list specific model names or credit amounts, so review the current plan details before relying on it for high-volume work. Commercial use requires a paid plan.

Best for: quick, versatile image generation across many styles, especially if you also plan to make video.

Midjourney has built its reputation on strong aesthetics. Images tend to arrive with polished composition, dramatic lighting and a distinctive painterly feel, which is why it is popular for concept art, mood boards, album-style visuals and editorial illustration. It offers style references and personalization, so you can steer results toward a consistent look across a project. It also supports editing and variation tools for refining a chosen image.

The trade-offs are practical. It is a paid service, and its prompts reward experimentation over literal instruction following, so you sometimes get something beautiful that is not exactly what you described.

Best for: artistic, high-impact visuals where mood matters more than exact specification.

Adobe Firefly focuses on professional workflows and commercial confidence. Adobe describes Firefly’s own models as trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it attaches Content Credentials metadata that records AI involvement. It connects with tools many teams already use, including Photoshop features like generative fill and generative expand, which suits designers who edit as much as they generate.

Firefly also provides controls such as style and composition references. Its results can feel cleaner and more commercial than Midjourney’s, which is an advantage for marketing assets and a limitation if you want a wild artistic look.

Best for: marketing and design teams that need editing tools and clearer licensing.

Ideogram is known for rendering legible text inside images, a task where many generators struggle. That makes it a strong choice for posters, social graphics, logo concepts, packaging mockups and product visuals that need a headline or short phrase to read correctly. It also offers style controls and a community gallery that doubles as a prompt library.

Even so, long paragraphs of on-image text can still go wrong. Keep the copy to a few words, put it in quotation marks in the prompt, and describe the lettering style.

Best for: graphics that combine imagery with short, readable text.

Leonardo AI is built for creators who want more control. It offers multiple models, fine-tuning options, image-to-image guidance and a canvas for editing, with a particular following among game artists and designers who need consistent characters and assets. Features such as reference-based generation help keep a character recognizable across many scenes.

The wide set of options is powerful but means a steeper learning curve than a one-box generator, and credit systems can take time to understand.

Best for: consistent characters, game and concept assets, and users who like tuning settings.

A reliable prompt has five parts. Put the most important part first, because it often carries the most weight.

How do text-to-image generators work? They convert your prompt into a numerical representation, then use a diffusion model to remove noise from a random starting image step by step, guided by that representation, until a matching picture appears.

Which text-to-image tool is best? It depends on the job. Pollo AI suits fast, varied generation, Midjourney suits artistic work, Adobe Firefly suits commercial design, Ideogram suits images with text and Leonardo AI suits tuned, consistent assets.

Why does the same prompt give different results? Each run starts from a different random seed. Fixing the seed, where a tool allows it, makes results more repeatable.

Can I use AI-generated images commercially? Often yes, but the rules differ by tool and plan. Pollo, for example, notes that commercial use requires a paid plan. Always check the current terms.

How do I get readable text in an AI image? Use a tool strong at text, keep the wording to a few words, and add the text in a design editor if accuracy is critical.

What file format should I download? WebP for lightweight web pages, PNG for graphics and sharp edges, JPEG for broad compatibility.

Can I turn a generated image into a video? Many platforms support it. Pollo AI, for example, also covers AI video, so you can move from a still to motion in one place.

Text-to-image generators work by turning language into numbers and using those numbers to guide a model that denoises random static into a picture. Once you understand that, prompts stop being guesswork: you give the model a clear subject, style and lighting, you iterate one change at a time, and you fix small flaws locally. Start with a versatile option such as Pollo AI, then add Midjourney, Firefly, Ideogram or Leonardo when a project needs their particular strengths.

#10401. Who wants 20 pounds of Trump coins?

If you want one of the U.S. Mint’s $1 coins featuring President Donald Trump’s portrait, you might need to purchase in bulk. The Mint announced its new limited-edition $1 Trump coins will be available beginning November 19 in 1,000-coin bags.

The 1,000-coin bags weigh about 20 pounds, and due to shipping weight constraints, there’s a maximum of two units per order, although there’s no household order limit. One bag costs $1,365 including shipping.

The Mint first released the $1 Trump coins in September, but the $65 25-coin roll and $154.50 100-coin bag formats that they were once available in are no longer in stock.

That means those looking to buy them will either have to purchase the 1,000-coin bag, or buy a 24-karat gold proof coin that comes in a clamshell case (the latter option will also be available November 19, though the Mint hasn’t said how much it will cost). The Mint says its mintage limit for the bags is 15,100, and 75,000 for the gold proof coin.

All told, that’s a lot of coins with a living president’s face on them for a country that traditionally doesn’t put living presidents on its money. Trump is the first to do it in a century (Calvin Coolidge was the last).

U.S. law has prohibited the country’s currency from depicting living presidents since 2005, but the Trump administration treated a 2020 law allowing for commemorative coins for the country’s 250th anniversary this year as a work-around to design a Trump coin.

Joseph Menna, chief engraver of the U.S. Mint, designed the coin. It shows Trump’s scowling face from his second-term official portrait taken by chief White House photographer Daniel Torok on the heads side along with the inscriptions for “Liberty,” “In God We Trust,” and “1776-2026.” The tails side shows the presidential seal. The coins are legal tender, though the Mint promotes them as commemorative collectibles.

A pair of Senate Democrats introduced the Change Corruption Act earlier this year, which would have prohibited the coin from being minted, but it was never brought up for a vote under the Republican-controlled Senate. Under Democratic control, Trump could have a harder time putting his face on U.S. money going forward.

With time running out, the Mint is putting out its Trump coins in bulk and at a discount. While the 1,000-coin bag is a bigger up-front payment, it’s also the cheapest these coins have been sold for. The 25-coin roll was sold at a 160% markup, and the 100-coin bag was sold at a 54.5% markup, while the 1,000-coin bag is being sold at a 36.5% markup. In the case of Trump’s coin, it costs money to spend money.

#10399. Homebuilders aren’t budging on prices. Instead, they’re quietly offering buyers much better deals

Homebuilders aren’t slashing prices on new homes, but they’ve found another way to entice buyers—they’re slashing mortgage rates.

Because affordability remains a key reason why many would-be homebuyers remain on the sidelines, builders are offering reduced mortgage rates to get people over the threshold. Americans who bought a new home paid an average starting mortgage rate of 5.01% in the third quarter, compared with a 6.15% rate for buyers of existing homes, according to a report released Tuesday by Realtor.com.

Such incentives aren’t new. Many builders have long leveraged their relationships with lenders or have offered mortgage rate buydowns to help buyers during periods of high interest rates. And even if the incentives are temporary, they can add up meaningfully: Austin-based Realtor.com estimates that homebuyers could save nearly $3,100 in interest on the purchase of a $400,000 home with a 10% down payment in the first year of homeownership compared with someone buying the same-priced existing home at the average starter rates. 

Though these sorts of adjustments aren’t reflected in the listing price, it shows how builders are adapting to the affordability challenges in the housing market, according to Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. “Reduced mortgage rates can help make a new home more affordable for buyers while allowing builders to hold asking prices relatively steady,” he said in a statement.

While reduced mortgage rate incentives are typically temporary, Realtor.com found that buyers of new homes are also securing lower 30-year fixed-rate mortgages than their peers buying existing homes—at 6.19% versus 6.68%. Over the lifetime of that mortgage, the new-home buyer would save more than $40,000 in interest.

“A temporary buydown can provide relief early on, while a lower rate fixed for the life of the loan offers a different kind of savings,” Berner said.

BUILDERS SLOW CONSTRUCTION

While affordability is a key theme in the housing market and, indeed, the broader economy right now, builders may be incentivized to move new homes for another reason: Construction activity has slowed.

The completion rate for new single-family homes fell 11% in September from the same period a year ago, Realtor.com found, and the inventory of new homes rose by only 0.1% in the third quarter from a year ago. As a result, newly constructed homes accounted for 16.7% of listings on the market in that period, down from 17.2% in 2025.

Homebuilders have been reluctant to reduce listing prices, which have remained largely steady in the past three years. But they’re grappling with a changing landscape. 

A gauge of homebuilder confidence fell to the lowest level in 14 years last month amid pressures like high mortgage rates and inflated construction and labor costs. That matched a slowdown in traffic of prospective buyers of newly constructed single-family homes, which fell to levels last seen in 2012, according to figures from the National Association of Home Builders and Wells Fargo.

The third-quarter earnings season was also tough for many homebuilders, including PulteGroup, which reported a decline in home sales revenue.

“The rapid increase in interest rates has stretched affordability even further, made selling an existing home even harder, and has pushed even more consumers to the sidelines,” Ryan Marshall, president and CEO of the Atlanta-based homebuilder, said in a statement.

#10398. Noodles & Company store closures: List of shuttered locations grows as restaurant chain optimizes footprint

Despite having closed dozens of restaurants in the last year, Noodles & Company has seen sales at remaining restaurants grow.

Executives at the fast-casual restaurant chain have pointed to a variety of reasons for the improvement. These include more customers dining at nearby locations after store closures; the addition of new, innovative dishes; and improved marketing and restaurant operations. 

How many Noodles & Company stores are closing?

In its third-quarter earnings release, the Colorado-based company said it now expects to close between 34 and 36 company-owned and seven to eight franchised restaurants this year, for a total of 41 to 44. (By comparison, Noodles & Company closed 33 company-owned restaurants in 2025.)

At the same time, it reported that system-wide comparable sales rose 9.5% in the third quarter.

“We continue to see a meaningful improvement in our restaurant-level economics related to our portfolio optimization project,” CFO Mike Hynes said on a November 13 earnings call.

Hynes said that during the third quarter, the company closed 12 company-owned restaurants and two franchised locations, and opened one new franchised restaurant.

Are more closures happening in 2027?

Hynes said the company doesn’t have firm numbers for 2027 closures, but its “best thinking right now would be 10-15 closures next year,” some of which would be natural lease expirations.

Overall, the fast-casual chain’s footprint has gotten smaller, third-quarter numbers reveal: As of September 29, the company had 383 restaurants: 306 company-owned and 77 franchised.

That’s down about 12% from 435 (349 company-owned and 86 franchised) a year earlier.

What Noodles & Company is doing to turn things around

Noodles & Company has enjoyed success with its ramen offerings. Its limited-time Chili Garlic Ramen dish attracted new and existing customers.

In October, the company made ramen a permanent menu category, adding Gochujang Carbonara Ramen Noodles, Sweet Sesame Steak Ramen Noodles, and Spicy Korean Steak Ramen Noodles.

The fast-casual eatery plans to rotate new ramen dishes to the lineup over time. 

As of Monday’s market close, shares of Noodles & Company (Nasdaq: NDLS) were up an impressive 60.4% year to date. However, the stock is down more than 30% over the last five days since its most recent earnings report.

#10393. The button-up was never designed for women’s bodies. These labels are fixing that

In the 1870s, tailors in London and Paris raced to redesign the most fundamental garment in a man’s wardrobe: the shirt.

Until then, men pulled shirts over their heads, with fabric that billowed down to their waist. But innovative shirt makers in Paris and London—like Charvet and Brown, Davis & Co.—realized that men wanted closer-fitting shirts. The breakthrough came when they sewed buttons down the front, along with darted seams and shoulder yokes, creating a flattering fit. As a final flourish, they added a stylish collar with pointed tips. And so the button-up shirt came into the world.

Over the next century, it would become one of the most iconic garments of our time. It conveyed good taste, but, perhaps more importantly, social status. A crisp, spotless shirt made it clear that the man wearing it didn’t work with his hands. He belonged to the professional class—what we’d later call a “white-collar worker.” From Tokyo to New York to Mumbai, dress shirts became a uniform at the office.

But in a strange twist, the shirt’s original customers have lost interest. Two-thirds of men now forego traditional workwear, opting for polos and t-shirts instead. But button-ups have found a new audience: women, who are dressing more formally even as men are becoming increasingly casual.

Search interest in women’s button-up shirts in the U.S. has more than doubled since 2019, according to Google Trends, and this April, it hit a 10-year high. The timing may not be a coincidence. Last year, McKinsey found that companies are retreating from their commitments to gender equity, giving women less support and fewer opportunities for advancement. As women are forced to advocate for themselves, it makes sense that they’re drawn to a garment historically linked to authority and competence.

The fashion industry is taking note. New labels have entered the market with a single mission of tailoring the dress shirt to the female form. Designers are tackling this issue in different ways: With Nothing Underneath keeps the masculine silhouette but subtly engineers it to a woman’s body, Frank & Eileen turns fine shirting fabrics historically reserved for men into styles that accentuate women’s curves, and TWP perfects the aesthetic of the oversized borrowed men’s shirt.

A century and a half later, tailors are once again racing to redesign the shirt. This time, it’s for women.

A Man’s Silhouette on a Woman’s Body

Women’s dress shirts aren’t new. Since the 1980s, brands have designed button-up shirts for women. But often, they try to feminize them with darts and cinched waists, designed to accentuate women’s hourglass form. This style isn’t everyone’s taste. Many women are drawn to the button-up shirt precisely because it is so masculine and represents male power.

Take Pip Durell, founder of a women’s shirting brand called With Nothing Underneath (WNU). In her career as a magazine editor at Vogue and Tatler, her uniform was jeans and a men’s dress shirt. In magazine shoots, she would call in men’s button-ups for female models, taking inspiration from the many women who have worn mens’ shirts with panache. (Coco Chanel famously borrowed her boyfriend’s shirts; Patti Smith wore a men’s shirt on the cover of her 1975 album Horses; Sharon Stone paired a men’s Gap shirt with a ball skirt at the 1998 Oscars.) “Men’s tailoring is impeccable,” says Phoebe Minney, WNU’s head of brand. “Savile Row has spent years perfecting the menswear wardrobe.”

The problem with wearing a men’s shirt is that it doesn’t hang the same way on a woman’s body. The shoulders are too broad and the sleeves are too long. The fabric stretches across the hips and gapes at the bust. In 2017, Durell decided to launch a label that would give women shirts that that would have the drape, fabric, and cut of a men’s shirt.

She began with a single style, the Boyfriend, that has oversized proportions and boxy lines. But under the surface, the brand has reengineered the shirt for women’s anatomy. Men’s shirts are cut wider in the front than in the back, to make room for their wide shoulders; WNU makes the back wider, so there is enough fabric on the front to make room for women’s busts. Buttons are strategically positioned so there is never a gape; the hem has extra length so it clears women’s wider hips and tucks easily. And the bottom buttonhole runs horizontally, so it stays fastened when tucked in. And while women’s shirts typically place their buttons on the left side, WNU’s shirts have their buttons on the right.

“Our buttons are still on the man’s side of the shirt as an homage to our inspiration,” says Minney.

Minney says that many of the brand’s customers are just entering the workforce and trying to figure out what to wear to their first corporate jobs as lawyers or bankers. At a time when even the most formal professions are relaxing their dress codes, a starched, slightly oversized dress shirt allows women to feel confident without being overdressed. And a white button-up with wide leg trousers is more comfortable than a suit. WNU designs its suits for movement to accommodate women’s busy lifestyles.

“Wealthy men whose shirts we’re modeling ours on might not have had to get on the tube every day, or carry their kids,” says Sarah Stokes, head of design at WNU. The brand’s design team obsesses over every detail of their shirts, focusing on places where they might come untucked or feel too tight. “The customer might not see the details on the hanger, but they feel them when they wear the shirts,” Stokes says. “We really overdevelop product.”

All of this obsession has given WNU a cult following. Both Kate Middleton and Meghan Markle are fans of the brand. Its core customer is a professional woman between 30 and 45 who wants a shirt that can carry her from a board meeting to the weekend. Shirts are priced between $175 and $250, which sits between mass market and luxury pricing. “You have the high street shirt that is poorly cut and not designed to last that long,” says Minney, the brand manager. “Then there’s really high end, where you’re looking at thousands for a shirt.”

There’s clearly a demand for WNU’s approach to shirt making. In 2022, WNU opened its first store, and in 2024, it raised its first outside funding. The company is now growing quickly in the United States. While it began venturing beyond shirts two years ago—including trousers, blazers, and denim—its focus remains on the shirt. Over the years, customers have asked for variations on the Boyfriend. WNU now has a portfolio, including the Classic, with a shorter, neater fit that tucks into trousers and slips under a blazer; the Weekend is more relaxed; the Q adds ruffles without being overly feminine.

Fine fabrics reserved for men

Frank & Eileen takes a very different approach. When Audrey McLoghlin launched the brand in 2009, she was less focused on fit, and entirely obsessed with materials.

McLoghlin trained as an engineer, then pivoted to a career in fashion, taking jobs at Gap and J.Crew. While at a factory in Los Angeles, she came across a book of Italian menswear fabrics on a dusty shelf. “All of a sudden, my mind was just blown,” she says. “Nobody makes button-ups for women out of these kinds of fabrics.”

For more than a century, Italy’s best mills have reserved their finest cottons and linens for men. By contrast, women’s shirts tended to be made from cheaper, coarser cotton or synthetics. The industry seemed to assume that women wouldn’t appreciate—or be willing to pay—for the drape or feel of these high-end fabrics. “These textiles are not an efficient solution,” says McLoghlin. “It’s really about the quality of the yarns and the love of the processes.”

With Frank & Eileen, McLoghlin wanted to take these male-coded materials and design them for a woman’s body. She found a 150-year-old mill that has made fabrics for some of the best-known menswear labels, and created shirts tailored to women’s curves. “I loved the contradiction of the masculine fabrics and heritage, then combining it with an extremely feminine silhouette,” she says. Her inspiration was less the boardroom, and more the Italian Riviera: the soft, lived-in shirt a man might wear day, after day, sleeves rolled, collar open.

Her first silhouette, the Barry, named after her father, took six months to develop with a pattern maker. Where WNU disguises its engineering, the Barry celebrates the female form. It curves in sharply at the sides and back. But the real flourish is at the top. The Barry has an open neckline designed to frame the face, and the buttons sit low enough that the collar stands up and the placket falls open without exposing too much. It also allows necklaces to stand out.

Five years later, after selling thousands of Barry shirts, Frank & Eileen launched the Eileen, which is almost its opposite. It has no structure, a soft shoulder, and a rounded body that covers the seat. This new design was partly a response to changing fashions. When skinny jeans dominated, women wanted long, loose shirts. Now that high-waisted trousers are back, tucking is in, and so is the Barry.

McLoghlin sees the button-up as a middle path between the 1980s power suit and the hoodie. Women once felt they had to show up in a suit with heels to command respect, she says. The shirt offers a quieter kind of authority. “It says, ‘I know who I am and I’ve earned my place at the table,’” she says.

Frank & Eileen spent its first decade in wholesale, selling through specialty stores and department stores such as Barneys New York and Ron Herman. In the pandemic, McLoghlin pivoted to selling directly to consumers, and e-commerce has since grown fivefold since 2021. Frank & Eileen has never taken outside investment. Last November, it opened its first U.S. flagship store in New York. Like WNU, it counts Meghan Markle as a fan. The Eileen, which retails for $288, now accounts for 30% of the business.

The romance of the borrowed shirt

There’s a fantasy attached to a woman wearing a men’s dress shirt: She wakes up after a rendezvous and pulls on his shirt, sleeves dangling past her wrists. This is the romance around which Trish Wescoat Pound built her eponymous brand. Pound founded TWP in 2021 after working at Theory and Michael Kors. The label grew out of “a void I saw in the market for the perfect white shirt,” she says. “And my love of a woman in an oversized shirt.”

You can see that wink in the shirt’s names, which include the Next Ex, the Soon To Be Ex, the Night We Met, the Next Morning, the Brief Encounter, and Something Borrowed. Beneath the cheekiness is a deeper ideas that the garment, and the authority it represents, can be co-opted by a woman.

Where WNU engineers the men’s shirt to fit women’s bodies, TWP revels in the places where a men’s shirt is too large for the female form. The oversized styles keep volume through the body and the long sleeves are perfect for rolling. But Pound obsesses over how to make these proportions look flattering, rather than swallowing the wearer. “There’s something about the ease of it, the borrowed-from-a-man aesthetic that I keep coming back to,” she says.

But in some ways, the shirts are a metaphor for women’s role in the workplace. Many women are looking for the perfect white shirt that allows them to project authority at work. Meanwhile, men can show up in hoodies and T-shirts without worrying that their competence will be questioned. Researchers call this the “red sneakers effect”: Dressing down signals status, but only for people whose authority is already assumed. Women rarely get that pass. One study found that women senior managers were judged less competent when their blouses were buttoned just one notch lower.

Men spent 150 years perfecting the dress shirt. Now, as they abandon it, women are claiming it for themselves. But this time, the borrowing comes with a twist. The shirt that once marked a man’s place in the professional class is being remade for women: cut for their bodies, sewn from fabrics once reserved for men, and, in TWP’s case, named with a wink at the men left behind.

#10392. Building Reliable Product Emails Into Your Application

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A password reset email is part of your login flow. An invoice notification is part of your billing experience. Yet development teams often treat these messages as background tasks: render a template, call a sending API, and move on. That approach leaves an important part of the product experience untested until a user cannot complete the action they started.

Testing the application interface alone leaves a gap. A successful request to an email provider does not establish that the recipient can find the message, understand it, or use its links. Product emails need explicit success criteria, useful diagnostic records, and recovery options when something fails.

A reliable workflow combines application tests, controlled mailbox checks, and pre-send diagnostics for authentication and inbox placement. A comparison of available tools can help you identify which checks your existing setup covers and where additional testing would be useful. The goal is to investigate specific gaps rather than add another service without a clear purpose.

Start with the action the recipient needs to complete. A weekly activity summary can tolerate a delay that would make a sign-in code useless. An invoice needs accurate amounts and a clear payment destination. A security alert needs enough context for someone to recognize the event without exposing sensitive information.

For each message, document its trigger, expected timing, required data, and expiration behavior. Decide what the application should display if submission fails or the user requests another copy. These decisions give developers and testers concrete acceptance criteria.

For a password reset, test the complete journey: requesting the message, receiving it in a controlled mailbox, following the link, and setting a new password. Also check what happens when the link expires or has already been used.

Template tests should cover the data your application actually encounters. Try long names, missing optional fields, non-Latin characters, and large order totals. Escape user-provided values appropriately, and make sure conditional sections disappear cleanly when their data is absent.

Inspect both HTML and plain-text versions. Instructions should remain understandable when images are blocked, while descriptive links and readable text should make the next action clear. Check that every URL points to the correct environment, especially when staging and production share template code.

A development sandbox lets you inspect generated messages without contacting customers. Use it to check headers, attachments, and content. Keep a separate rendering check for the email clients your audience uses, because a sandbox preview cannot reproduce every client’s behavior.

A background queue can prevent a slow sending API from delaying a web request. It also creates another failure boundary: a worker may time out after the provider has accepted the email but before your application records the result.

If the job retries blindly, the recipient may receive two messages. Assign a stable identifier to each logical notification and record the provider’s message identifier when available. Where supported, reuse an idempotency key for retries of the same send operation, following the provider’s documented retention window.

Distinguish retries from intentional resends. A user asking for a new reset link is a different event from a worker repeating an uncertain request. Define which link remains valid when another is issued, and test that behavior explicitly.

Retries also need limits. Temporary service failures may justify another attempt with backoff. A permanently invalid address needs a correction or suppression workflow, rather than repeated sending.

Provider events describe different stages of the sending process. An acceptance response means the provider accepted the request. A delivery event generally means the receiving mail server accepted the message; it does not prove inbox placement or that a person read it.

Capture the events your provider exposes, including bounces, delays, and complaints. Associate them with the original notification so support staff can investigate a particular report. Confirm each event’s documented meaning instead of treating similar labels across providers as interchangeable.

Webhook handlers should verify incoming requests using the provider’s documented mechanism and tolerate duplicate notifications. Avoid assuming events always arrive in chronological order. Record enough history to explain what happened without allowing a late event to overwrite a more informative state.

Before releasing a significant template or infrastructure change, send controlled messages through the production sending configuration to test accounts at commonly used mailbox providers. Use synthetic data, and check placement, rendering, link behavior, and how long the message takes to arrive.

Inspect authentication results in the received headers. Published DNS records are only part of the configuration; the actual message must use the expected signing domain and sending infrastructure. If you change providers or domains, repeat these checks rather than assuming the previous results still apply.

Treat test mailbox results as samples. They can reveal problems, but they cannot guarantee identical placement for every recipient. Mailbox settings, filtering decisions, and recipient history can produce different outcomes.

Provide a resend option with sensible rate limits and explain when users should expect the message. Where appropriate, let signed-in users verify or correct their address. For public account-recovery forms, avoid responses that reveal whether a particular address has an account.

Give support staff a way to distinguish a notification that was never generated from a failed submission or a message accepted by the receiving server. Protect that diagnostic access, limit retention, and avoid logging reset tokens, private message bodies, or unnecessary personal information.

Reliable product email depends on the whole journey, from the triggering event to the recipient’s next action. Testing each stage and making failures observable helps teams resolve problems before users repeatedly click resend or abandon the task.
